title: Computer Vision for Robots

mentor.name: IRIS-8
mentor.character: Shows you the frame before the theory, then makes you prove the number you read off it.

summary: You will build every stage a robot needs to see: color segmentation, contours and centroids, edges and lines, feature matching, camera calibration, ArUco pose, stereo depth, optical flow and tracking. By the end you assemble a pick and place vision node that reports grasp poses in millimetres and refuses to guess when perception fails.

lessons.title: Opening the Eye
lessons.goal: Load an image file into memory with OpenCV and verify that the load actually worked.
lessons.theory:
A robot camera is useless until the frame reaches your code. In Python the entry point is `cv2.imread(path)`, which returns a **NumPy array** when it succeeds and `None` when it fails. It fails silently: a wrong path, a missing file or an unsupported codec all give you `None` with no exception.

That silence is the first bug every vision student ships. On a rover the camera file may not exist yet because the driver has not mounted the device, and your pipeline will crash three functions later with a confusing error about `NoneType`. Check the return value at the source.

OpenCV also loads in **BGR** order, not RGB. That is a historical quirk from the library's early Intel days and it never changed. Every function in this course assumes BGR, so only convert when you hand the array to something else, like Matplotlib or a neural network.
lessons.task: Load `bench.jpg` with `cv2.imread`, and if the result is `None`, raise a `FileNotFoundError` with the path in the message instead of continuing.
lessons.starter:
import cv2

path = "bench.jpg"
frame = cv2.imread(path)

# TODO: refuse to continue when the camera gave nothing back

print("loaded")
lessons.solution:
import cv2

path = "bench.jpg"
frame = cv2.imread(path)

if frame is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"camera frame not available: {path}")

print("loaded")
lessons.hint: `cv2.imread` never throws, so the only way to know it failed is comparing the result against `None` with `is`.

lessons.title: The Grid Behind the Picture
lessons.goal: Read the height, width and channel count of a frame from its shape tuple.
lessons.theory:
An image in OpenCV is a NumPy array of shape `(height, width, channels)`. Note the order: **rows first**. A 1280x720 camera gives you `frame.shape == (720, 1280, 3)`. Half the off by one bugs in robot vision come from someone writing `w, h = frame.shape[:2]`.

The `dtype` matters as much as the shape. A normal camera frame is `uint8`, so every value lives between 0 and 255 and arithmetic **wraps around**: 250 plus 10 gives 4, not 260. When you start averaging frames or computing gradients you will convert to `float32` first, on purpose.

A grayscale image has only two entries in `shape`, because there is no channel axis at all. Code that blindly unpacks three values breaks the moment someone feeds it a mask.
lessons.task: Unpack height and width from `frame.shape` in the correct order and print them, then print the dtype. Handle the case where the array has no channel axis.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

# TODO: unpack the frame dimensions in the order the array actually stores them
print(frame.dtype)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

height, width = frame.shape[:2]
channels = frame.shape[2] if frame.ndim == 3 else 1

print(height, width, channels)
print(frame.dtype)
lessons.hint: Slice the tuple with `frame.shape[:2]` and remember that rows come before columns.

lessons.title: Cutting the Field of View
lessons.goal: Extract a region of interest from a frame using NumPy slicing.
lessons.theory:
A region of interest, or **ROI**, is just a NumPy slice: `roi = frame[y0:y1, x0:x1]`. Rows before columns again. No pixels are copied, you get a **view** into the same memory, so writing into the ROI writes into the original frame. Use `.copy()` when you want an independent buffer.

ROIs are the cheapest speed trick in robot vision. A line following rover only cares about the bottom third of the image, the part of the floor two meters ahead. Cropping to that strip cuts the pixel count by two thirds before any filter runs, which on a Raspberry Pi 5 is the difference between 12 and 30 frames per second.

Slices outside the image do not raise an error, NumPy clamps them, so an ROI can come back empty. Check `roi.size` before you trust it.
lessons.task: Build a `bottom_strip` view holding the lowest third of the frame, full width, and print its shape.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
height, width = frame.shape[:2]

# TODO: slice the bottom third of the frame
bottom_strip = frame

print(bottom_strip.shape)
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
height, width = frame.shape[:2]

y0 = (height * 2) // 3
bottom_strip = frame[y0:height, 0:width]

if bottom_strip.size == 0:
    raise ValueError("empty region of interest")

print(bottom_strip.shape)
lessons.hint: The first row of the bottom third is at two thirds of the height, and the slice keeps every column.

lessons.title: Marks on the Glass
lessons.goal: Draw rectangles, circles and text on a frame to build a debug overlay.
lessons.theory:
You cannot attach a debugger to a moving robot, so the frame itself becomes your console. OpenCV draws in place with `cv2.rectangle`, `cv2.circle`, `cv2.line` and `cv2.putText`, all of them modifying the array you pass in.

Coordinates in drawing calls are `(x, y)`, the opposite order of array indexing. This inconsistency inside the same library is a real source of bugs, and the only defense is naming your variables `x` and `y` instead of `a` and `b`. Colors are BGR tuples, so pure red is `(0, 0, 255)`.

Always draw on a copy when the original frame feeds the next stage of the pipeline. A green rectangle burnt into the source image will be found later by your own color detector, and you will spend an afternoon chasing a phantom object.
lessons.task: Copy the frame, draw a rectangle around the detection box given by `x, y, w, h`, mark its center with a filled circle, and label it with `cv2.putText`.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((480, 640, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
x, y, w, h = 200, 150, 120, 90

overlay = frame.copy()
# TODO: draw the box, its center and a text label on overlay

print(overlay.shape)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((480, 640, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
x, y, w, h = 200, 150, 120, 90

overlay = frame.copy()
cv2.rectangle(overlay, (x, y), (x + w, y + h), (0, 255, 0), 2)
cv2.circle(overlay, (x + w // 2, y + h // 2), 4, (0, 0, 255), -1)
cv2.putText(overlay, "part", (x, y - 8), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.6, (0, 255, 0), 2)

print(overlay.shape)
lessons.hint: `cv2.rectangle` wants the top left and bottom right corners, and a thickness of -1 fills a shape.

lessons.title: The Stream Never Stops
lessons.goal: Read frames from a camera in a loop and release the device cleanly.
lessons.theory:
A robot does not process one photo, it processes a stream. `cv2.VideoCapture(0)` opens the first video device, `cap.read()` returns `(ok, frame)` on every call, and `ok` going false means the device dropped, the USB cable moved or the file ended. Treat a false `ok` as a sensor failure, not as end of program.

Set the resolution before the loop with `cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)`. A cheap UVC webcam will happily give you 1920x1080 that your pipeline cannot process in time, and a queue of stale frames is worse than a low resolution one: the robot reacts to where the object was half a second ago.

Always call `cap.release()`. On Linux a leaked capture keeps `/dev/video0` busy, and the next launch of your node fails to open the camera for no visible reason.
lessons.task: Write a capture loop that reads up to 100 frames, breaks out when `ok` is false, counts the frames it got, and releases the device in a `finally` block.
lessons.starter:
import cv2

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480)

count = 0
# TODO: read up to 100 frames, stop early if a read fails, release no matter what

print(count)
lessons.solution:
import cv2

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_WIDTH, 640)
cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT, 480)

count = 0
try:
    if not cap.isOpened():
        raise RuntimeError("camera device did not open")
    for _ in range(100):
        ok, frame = cap.read()
        if not ok:
            break
        height, width = frame.shape[:2]
        count += 1
finally:
    cap.release()

print(count)
lessons.hint: `cap.read()` returns two values, and the release belongs in `finally` so it runs even when the loop raises.

lessons.title: Three Planes of Light
lessons.goal: Split a BGR frame into its channels and rebuild it with merge.
lessons.theory:
A color frame is three grayscale images stacked on the last axis. `cv2.split(frame)` hands you `b, g, r` as separate 2D arrays and `cv2.merge((b, g, r))` puts them back. Slicing with `frame[:, :, 2]` gives the same red plane without copying, which is faster inside a loop.

Channels are not equally useful. On a warehouse floor lit by sodium lamps the blue plane is almost pure noise, while the red plane carries most of the contrast. Looking at the planes separately is the fastest way to understand what your camera actually sees before you design a filter.

Swapping channels is also the cheapest way to convert to RGB for a library that expects it: `frame[:, :, ::-1]`. That reversal is a view, not a conversion, so it costs nothing until something copies it.
lessons.task: Split the frame, print the mean of each channel, then rebuild a frame with the blue and red planes swapped.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((240, 320, 3), (40, 90, 200), dtype=np.uint8)

# TODO: split into b, g, r, print the means, merge back swapped
swapped = frame

print(swapped.shape)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((240, 320, 3), (40, 90, 200), dtype=np.uint8)

b, g, r = cv2.split(frame)
print(round(b.mean(), 2), round(g.mean(), 2), round(r.mean(), 2))

swapped = cv2.merge((r, g, b))
print(swapped.shape)
lessons.hint: `cv2.split` returns the planes in BGR order, so the first one out is blue.

lessons.title: Draining the Color
lessons.goal: Convert a frame to grayscale and explain why the channel weights are not equal.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)` collapses three planes into one using `0.299*R + 0.587*G + 0.114*B`. Those weights come from human luminance perception: the eye has far more green sensitive cones than blue ones. A plain average of the three channels looks wrong, dark reds go too bright and greens go flat.

Grayscale is where most of the classical pipeline lives. Edges, corners, template matching and feature descriptors all work on a single plane, because a gradient in three channels has no unambiguous direction. Converting early also cuts memory traffic by two thirds.

The cost is information you cannot get back. A red emergency stop button and a green ready lamp of the same brightness become the same gray. When color **is** the signal, stay in color and go to HSV instead.
lessons.task: Convert the frame to grayscale with `cvtColor`, then compute the same value manually with the luminance weights and print the largest difference between the two.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 256, (120, 160, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

gray = None
# TODO: convert with cvtColor and reproduce it with the weights

print(gray.shape if gray is not None else None)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 256, (120, 160, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

b, g, r = cv2.split(frame.astype(np.float32))
manual = 0.299 * r + 0.587 * g + 0.114 * b

diff = np.abs(manual - gray.astype(np.float32)).max()
print(gray.shape, round(float(diff), 3))
lessons.hint: Cast to `float32` before the weighted sum or the uint8 arithmetic will wrap around.

lessons.title: The Hue Wheel
lessons.goal: Convert to HSV and read the meaning of the hue, saturation and value channels.
lessons.theory:
**HSV** separates what color something is from how bright it is. Hue is the angle on the color wheel, saturation is how far the color is from gray, value is brightness. OpenCV packs hue into a `uint8`, so the 0 to 360 degree wheel is halved: hue runs **0 to 179**, while saturation and value run 0 to 255. The conversion itself is `cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)`, where `cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV` is the code that tells `cvtColor` which space the frame starts in and which one it lands in.

This separation is why every color tracker in robotics uses HSV instead of BGR. A yellow tennis ball under a bright lamp and the same ball in shadow have wildly different BGR triples but almost the same hue. You gate hue tightly and leave saturation and value loose, and the tracker survives the lighting changing across the room.

Hue is meaningless when saturation is near zero. White walls, gray metal and black rubber all produce random hue values, which is why every practical gate includes a saturation floor around 80.
lessons.task: Convert the frame to HSV, split it, and print the mean hue only over the pixels whose saturation is above 80.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((200, 200, 3), (0, 200, 255), dtype=np.uint8)

# TODO: convert to HSV, split, and average hue where saturation is high
mean_hue = 0.0

print(round(mean_hue, 2))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((200, 200, 3), (0, 200, 255), dtype=np.uint8)

hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
h, s, v = cv2.split(hsv)

saturated = s > 80
mean_hue = float(h[saturated].mean()) if np.any(saturated) else 0.0

print(round(mean_hue, 2))
lessons.hint: Boolean indexing with `h[s > 80]` keeps only the pixels whose color is worth trusting.

lessons.title: The Seam in the Wheel
lessons.goal: Handle the red hue wraparound by splitting the range in two.
lessons.theory:
Red sits at hue 0, which is also hue 179. The wheel is circular but a numeric range is not, so a single `low <= h <= high` test can never cover red. Beginners write `0 to 10` and lose every slightly pink pixel, or write `170 to 179` and lose the rest.

The fix is two ranges: roughly `0 to 10` and `170 to 179`, tested separately and combined. Every other color needs only one range, red is the single special case, and it happens to be the color of most emergency stops, warning tape and calibration targets in a workshop.

Rotating the hue channel before gating is an alternative trick: adding 90 modulo 180 moves red to the middle of the range. It costs one array operation per frame and removes the special case entirely, which is worth it when the same code has to handle any color a user picks.
lessons.task: Write `red_hue_mask(h)` that returns a boolean array true for hues in either red band, and print how many pixels it selects.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np

h = np.array([0, 5, 90, 120, 175, 179], dtype=np.uint8)

def red_hue_mask(h):
    # TODO: cover both ends of the wheel
    return h < 10

print(int(red_hue_mask(h).sum()))
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np

h = np.array([0, 5, 90, 120, 175, 179], dtype=np.uint8)

def red_hue_mask(h):
    low_band = (h >= 0) & (h <= 10)
    high_band = (h >= 170) & (h <= 179)
    return low_band | high_band

print(int(red_hue_mask(h).sum()))
lessons.hint: A `low_band` and a `high_band` joined with `|`, in that order, and remember NumPy needs parentheses around each side.

lessons.title: Light That Lies
lessons.goal: Use the LAB color space to separate lightness from color for illumination robustness.
lessons.theory:
**LAB** splits a frame into L, perceptual lightness, and two color axes: A running green to red, B running blue to yellow. Unlike HSV, distance in the A and B plane is roughly proportional to perceived color difference, which makes it the right space for asking how similar two colors are.

On a robot this buys you illumination robustness in a different way than HSV. If you keep only A and B and throw away L, a conveyor belt lit by a window at noon and by fluorescent tubes at night produces nearly the same numbers. HSV degrades faster because its saturation still depends on brightness.

LAB is also how you fix uneven lighting cheaply: run CLAHE on the L channel only, merge back, and the color stays untouched while the shadows lift. The trip back is `cv2.COLOR_LAB2BGR`, the mirror of `cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB`.

Both halves of that claim are measurable, so measure them instead of trusting the shape of the array. The lift shows up in the shaded strip of the frame: its mean L and its spread both rise. The color claim shows up as chroma drift, the largest change in A or B after the round trip through BGR. Touching L only leaves a drift of one or two levels, which is nothing but uint8 rounding. Running CLAHE on all three channels instead pushes that drift an order of magnitude higher, and that is the lurid oversaturated look you see in bad demos.
lessons.task: Convert to LAB, apply `cv2.createCLAHE` to the L channel only, merge back and convert to BGR. Then print the proof: the mean and spread of L in the shaded strip before and after, and the chroma drift of the L only frame next to the drift you get when CLAHE runs on all three channels.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

shade = np.linspace(0.25, 1.0, 200, dtype=np.float32)
frame = np.zeros((200, 200, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
frame[:, :, 0] = 40
frame[:, :, 1] = 90
frame[:, :, 2] = 160
frame = (frame * shade[None, :, None]).astype(np.uint8)
shadow = slice(0, 50)

lab = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB)
l, a, b = cv2.split(lab)

# TODO: equalize only L, rebuild the BGR frame, and measure the lift and the color drift
l_fixed = l

print("shadow L mean", round(float(l[:, shadow].mean()), 1), "->", round(float(l_fixed[:, shadow].mean()), 1))
print("shadow L spread", int(l[:, shadow].max()) - int(l[:, shadow].min()), "->", int(l_fixed[:, shadow].max()) - int(l_fixed[:, shadow].min()))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

shade = np.linspace(0.25, 1.0, 200, dtype=np.float32)
frame = np.zeros((200, 200, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
frame[:, :, 0] = 40
frame[:, :, 1] = 90
frame[:, :, 2] = 160
frame = (frame * shade[None, :, None]).astype(np.uint8)
shadow = slice(0, 50)

lab = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB)
l, a, b = cv2.split(lab)

clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
l_fixed = clahe.apply(l)

fixed = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.merge((l_fixed, a, b)), cv2.COLOR_LAB2BGR)
all_three = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.merge((l_fixed, clahe.apply(a), clahe.apply(b))), cv2.COLOR_LAB2BGR)

def chroma_drift(bgr):
    _, ca, cb = cv2.split(cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB))
    return int(max(np.abs(ca.astype(np.int32) - a).max(), np.abs(cb.astype(np.int32) - b).max()))

print("shadow L mean", round(float(l[:, shadow].mean()), 1), "->", round(float(l_fixed[:, shadow].mean()), 1))
print("shadow L spread", int(l[:, shadow].max()) - int(l[:, shadow].min()), "->", int(l_fixed[:, shadow].max()) - int(l_fixed[:, shadow].min()))
print("chroma drift L only", chroma_drift(fixed))
print("chroma drift all three", chroma_drift(all_three))
lessons.hint: CLAHE takes a single channel, so split first and only touch the one that carries lightness. For the drift, send each finished BGR frame back to LAB and compare its A and B against the a and b you split out at the start.

lessons.title: Gain Without Blowing Out
lessons.goal: Adjust brightness and contrast with convertScaleAbs and with a gamma lookup table.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.convertScaleAbs(frame, alpha, beta)` computes `alpha * pixel + beta` and clips to 0 to 255. Alpha is contrast gain, beta is a brightness offset. It is linear, so it lifts shadows and highlights by the same factor and clips the bright end quickly.

**Gamma correction** is the nonlinear alternative: `output = 255 * (pixel / 255) ** gamma`. Gamma below 1 lifts the dark end while barely touching the bright end, which is exactly what you want when a robot drives from a lit aisle into a shadowed rack. Computing that power per pixel is slow, so you precompute a 256 entry lookup table once and apply it with `cv2.LUT`, which is a memory read per pixel.

Neither of these adds information. If the sensor clipped to 255 the data is gone. Fix exposure on the camera first, use these to make an already decent frame easier for the next stage.
lessons.task: Build a 256 entry gamma table for gamma 0.5, apply it with `cv2.LUT`, and also produce a linear version with `convertScaleAbs` at alpha 1.4. Print the mean of the original frame next to both results, because the whole point is which of the two lifts a dark frame further.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 120, (100, 100, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
gamma = 0.5

# TODO: build the lookup table and apply it, then do the linear version
brightened = frame
linear = frame

print(int(frame.mean()), int(brightened.mean()), int(linear.mean()))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 120, (100, 100, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
gamma = 0.5

table = np.array([((i / 255.0) ** gamma) * 255 for i in range(256)], dtype=np.uint8)
brightened = cv2.LUT(frame, table)

linear = cv2.convertScaleAbs(frame, alpha=1.4, beta=0)

print(int(frame.mean()), int(brightened.mean()), int(linear.mean()))
lessons.hint: The table has one entry per possible input value, and `cv2.LUT` maps every pixel through it in one pass.

lessons.title: White Balance on the Rover
lessons.goal: Correct a color cast with the gray world assumption before any color gate runs.
lessons.theory:
The **gray world** assumption says that averaged over a whole scene, the world is neutral gray. If your frame's blue mean is much higher than its red mean, the light is blue, not the world. Scale each channel so all three means match and the cast disappears.

This matters because every threshold you tune in the lab is tuned under lab light. Move the robot outdoors at sunset and the same orange cone lands in a different hue bucket. One cheap white balance pass in front of the color gate saves you from retuning the gate for every room.

The assumption breaks when one color dominates the frame legitimately, a camera pointed at a green lawn will be dragged toward magenta. Guard it: only apply the correction when the channel means differ by less than a factor of two, otherwise leave the frame alone.
lessons.task: Write `gray_world(frame)` that scales each channel so its mean equals the overall mean, clipping to uint8, and returns the frame unchanged when any channel mean is zero.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((120, 120, 3), (200, 120, 80), dtype=np.uint8)

def gray_world(frame):
    # TODO: scale each channel toward the global mean
    return frame

out = gray_world(frame)
print([int(out[:, :, i].mean()) for i in range(3)])
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((120, 120, 3), (200, 120, 80), dtype=np.uint8)

def gray_world(frame):
    planes = cv2.split(frame.astype(np.float32))
    means = [p.mean() for p in planes]
    if min(means) < 1.0:
        return frame
    target = sum(means) / 3.0
    scaled = [np.clip(p * (target / m), 0, 255) for p, m in zip(planes, means)]
    return cv2.merge(scaled).astype(np.uint8)

out = gray_world(frame)
print([int(out[:, :, i].mean()) for i in range(3)])
lessons.hint: Each channel gets its own gain: the global mean divided by that channel's mean.

lessons.title: Shrinking the World
lessons.goal: Resize frames with the right interpolation flag for shrinking and for growing.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.resize(frame, (width, height))` takes the target size as `(w, h)`, the opposite order of `shape`. When shrinking, use `cv2.INTER_AREA`: it averages the source pixels that fall into each output pixel, which is a proper low pass filter and avoids aliasing. When growing, `cv2.INTER_LINEAR` is the default and `cv2.INTER_CUBIC` is sharper and slower.

Downscaling is the single biggest performance lever in a vision pipeline. Going from 1280x720 to 640x360 removes 75 percent of the pixels and most stages scale linearly with pixel count. A tennis ball 40 pixels wide is still 20 pixels wide after the halving, more than enough for a color blob detector.

Remember that every coordinate you compute on the small frame must be scaled back before it reaches the robot. Keep the scale factor in a variable next to the resize, never as a magic number three functions away.
lessons.task: Halve the frame with the interpolation meant for shrinking, then write `to_full(x, y)` that maps a point from the small frame back to full resolution.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
scale = 0.5

# TODO: resize with the right flag and write the coordinate mapping back
small = frame

print(small.shape)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((720, 1280, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
scale = 0.5

height, width = frame.shape[:2]
small = cv2.resize(frame, (int(width * scale), int(height * scale)), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)

def to_full(x, y):
    return int(x / scale), int(y / scale)

print(small.shape, to_full(100, 50))
lessons.hint: `cv2.INTER_AREA` for shrinking, and the size argument is a `(width, height)` tuple.

lessons.title: The Camera Is Mounted Upside Down
lessons.goal: Correct mounting orientation with flip and rotate before the pipeline sees the frame.
lessons.theory:
Cameras get bolted wherever the chassis allows. A Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 under a rover deck usually ends up rotated 180 degrees, and a downward facing gripper camera often ends up mirrored. `cv2.flip(frame, 0)` flips vertically, `1` horizontally, `-1` both. `cv2.rotate` handles the three multiples of 90 degrees without interpolation.

Fix orientation **once**, immediately after `cap.read()`, and never again. If you compensate inside each detector you will eventually miss one, and a mirrored frame breaks anything chiral: text becomes unreadable, ArUco markers stop decoding, and a left turn command steers right.

Arbitrary angles need `cv2.warpAffine` with a matrix from `cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, angle, 1.0)`. That one interpolates, so it costs quality and time, and it is only worth it when the mount really is tilted 12 degrees and you cannot reach the screws.

import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((480, 640, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
frame[:120, :160] = (255, 255, 255)

def badge_center(image):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    moments = cv2.moments((gray > 127).astype(np.uint8))
    return int(round(moments["m10"] / moments["m00"])), int(round(moments["m01"] / moments["m00"]))

def fix_mount(frame):
    return cv2.rotate(frame, cv2.ROTATE_180)

height, width = frame.shape[:2]
center = (width // 2, height // 2)
matrix = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, 12.0, 1.0)
tilted = cv2.warpAffine(frame, matrix, (width, height))

print(badge_center(frame), badge_center(fix_mount(frame)), badge_center(tilted))
lessons.hint: `cv2.ROTATE_180` needs no interpolation, while any other angle goes through `getRotationMatrix2D` and `warpAffine`. A 180 degree rotation sends the pixel at `(x, y)` to `(width - 1 - x, height - 1 - y)`, so the badge center is the cheapest proof that the frame really turned.

chapters.title: Black, White and the Line Between

lessons.title: The Cut
lessons.goal: Apply a fixed global threshold to turn a grayscale frame into a binary mask.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)` returns two things: the threshold actually used and the binary image. Every pixel above 127 becomes 255, everything else becomes 0. That is the whole operation, and it is the foundation of every classical detector in this course.

A binary mask is what turns pixels into objects. Counting, measuring, finding contours and computing a centroid all need a clean yes or no per pixel. Grayscale has 256 answers per pixel, and none of them tells you where the part ends.

A fixed threshold is brittle by design. It works when you control the light, for example a backlit inspection jig where the part is a black silhouette on a bright LED panel. Move that jig near a window and the number 127 becomes wrong. That is why the next three lessons exist.
lessons.task: Convert to grayscale, threshold at 127 in binary mode, print the fraction of white pixels, and also produce the inverted mask with `THRESH_BINARY_INV`.
lessons.starter:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 256, (200, 200, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
# TODO: threshold at 127 and build the inverted mask too
mask = gray

print(round(float((mask > 0).mean()), 3))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
frame = rng.integers(0, 256, (200, 200, 3), dtype=np.uint8)

gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

used, mask = cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
_, mask_inv = cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV)

lessons.hint: `cv2.threshold` returns a tuple, so unpack it as `used, mask = ...` instead of assigning the whole thing.

lessons.title: Letting the Histogram Decide
lessons.goal: Pick the threshold automatically with Otsu's method instead of hardcoding a number.
lessons.theory:
**Otsu's method** looks at the histogram of the grayscale image and searches for the cut that minimises the variance inside each of the two resulting groups. In plain terms: it finds the valley between two peaks. You request it with `cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU` and pass 0 as the threshold, because the algorithm overrides it. The value it chose comes back as the first return value, and printing it is the fastest way to know whether the scene really is bimodal.

Otsu assumes two populations of pixels, background and foreground, with a real gap between them. A silhouette on a light table fits perfectly. A cluttered warehouse aisle does not, and Otsu will still return a number, confidently, in the middle of nothing.

Blur before Otsu. A 5x5 Gaussian smooths the histogram and stops sensor noise from creating fake valleys. This is one of the few places where a preprocessing step reliably improves an automatic decision.
lessons.task: Blur the grayscale image with a 5x5 Gaussian, run Otsu, and print the threshold value the algorithm selected.
lessons.starter:
import cv2
import numpy as np

gray = np.concatenate([np.full((100, 200), 40, np.uint8), np.full((100, 200), 210, np.uint8)])

# TODO: blur, then threshold with Otsu and print the chosen value
chosen = 0

print(chosen)
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

gray = np.concatenate([np.full((100, 200), 40, np.uint8), np.full((100, 200), 210, np.uint8)])

blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
chosen, mask = cv2.threshold(blurred, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

print(int(chosen), round(float((mask > 0).mean()), 3))
lessons.hint: Pass 0 as the threshold argument and add `cv2.THRESH_OTSU` to the mode flag.

lessons.title: Shadow on the Bench
lessons.goal: Use adaptive thresholding when the lighting changes across the frame.
lessons.theory:
One number cannot serve a frame where the left side is lit by a lamp and the right side is in the arm's shadow. `cv2.adaptiveThreshold` computes a **different threshold for every pixel** from its neighbourhood: `ADAPTIVE_THRESH_MEAN_C` uses the mean of a block, `ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C` uses a weighted mean.

Two parameters control it. `blockSize` must be odd and should be clearly larger than the features you want to keep: 11 to 31 for printed labels, 51 or more for wide parts. `C` is a constant subtracted from the local mean, and it is what removes the salt in flat areas. Start with `C` around 5 and raise it when the background comes out speckled.

Adaptive thresholding is the right tool for reading a shipping label under a gripper camera or finding a black line on a floor that a window brightens near noon. It cannot recover contrast that does not exist locally: a part the same brightness as the table beside it stays invisible no matter the block size.
lessons.task: Apply Gaussian adaptive thresholding with a block size of 25 and a C of 5, in inverted binary mode so the dark line becomes white. Print how many pixels the adaptive mask keeps next to how many one global Otsu threshold keeps on the same lit gradient.

gray[:, 140:152] = np.clip(gray[:, 140:152].astype(np.int16) - 60, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

_, global_mask = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

# TODO: threshold every pixel against its own neighbourhood so the gradient stops mattering

import numpy as np

lessons.title: The Color Gate
lessons.goal: Isolate an object by color with cv2.inRange over an HSV frame.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.inRange(hsv, lower, upper)` returns a mask that is 255 where **every** channel falls inside its band and 0 anywhere else. The bounds are NumPy arrays of three values, and in HSV they mean hue, saturation, value in that order.

This is the workhorse of robot color tracking. To follow an orange traffic cone you gate hue around 10 to 25, saturation from 120 up to 255 and value from 70 up to 255. The tight band is on hue, the loose bands are on the other two, because those are the ones the lighting moves.

Do not tune these numbers by guessing. Point the camera at the object, print the median hue and saturation over a small central patch, and build the bounds around what you measured. Twenty seconds of measurement beats an hour of sliding trackbars.
lessons.task: Write `color_gate(frame, hue, tolerance)` that converts to HSV and returns the `inRange` mask for that hue with a saturation floor of 120 and a value floor of 70.

def color_gate(frame, hue, tolerance):
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
    # TODO: build the lower and upper bounds and return the mask
    return np.zeros(frame.shape[:2], np.uint8)

mask = color_gate(frame, 15, 8)
print(int(cv2.countNonZero(mask)))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((150, 150, 3), (0, 140, 230), dtype=np.uint8)

def color_gate(frame, hue, tolerance):
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
    lower = np.array([max(0, hue - tolerance), 120, 70], dtype=np.uint8)
    upper = np.array([min(179, hue + tolerance), 255, 255], dtype=np.uint8)
    return cv2.inRange(hsv, lower, upper)

mask = color_gate(frame, 15, 8)
print(int(cv2.countNonZero(mask)))
lessons.hint: Both bounds are three element uint8 arrays, and hue must stay clamped between 0 and 179.

lessons.title: Masks That Multiply
lessons.goal: Apply a binary mask to a color frame with bitwise_and to keep only the object.
lessons.theory:
A mask alone tells you where the object is. `cv2.bitwise_and(frame, frame, mask=mask)` gives you the object itself, with everything outside the mask set to black. The doubled first argument looks strange but is correct: the AND is of the frame with itself, and the `mask` keyword is what restricts where the operation happens.

This matters when a later stage needs the original pixels, not just the geometry. Measuring the average color of a detected part to tell a red bolt from an orange one needs the masked frame. Computing a histogram of only the object needs it too.

Every bitwise function in OpenCV accepts that `mask` keyword, and every one of them requires the mask to be single channel `uint8` with the same height and width as the frame. A mask of the wrong dtype gives an assertion error that names the wrong argument, so check the mask first when that appears.
lessons.task: Apply the mask to the frame with `bitwise_and`, then print the mean color of the object using the mask next to the mean of the whole frame, so you can read off how far the background was dragging the average down.

lessons.title: Two Gates, One Object
lessons.goal: Combine masks with bitwise_or and bitwise_not to detect a color that wraps the hue wheel.
lessons.theory:
Red needs two `inRange` calls, one near hue 0 and one near hue 179, joined with `cv2.bitwise_or`. That is the practical form of the wraparound you handled with boolean arrays earlier, now expressed in the OpenCV functions that run at full speed on a whole frame.

The other two combinators complete the toolkit. `cv2.bitwise_and` of two masks keeps only what both agree on, which is how you require a pixel to be both the right color and inside the workspace rectangle. `cv2.bitwise_not` inverts, which is how you build a background mask from a foreground one.

A robot that must stop for a red emergency marker painted on the floor lives on exactly this: two hue bands, an OR, an AND with the floor region of interest, and a pixel count. No neural network is going to beat that on a 30 dollar compute module.
lessons.task: Build a red mask from two hue bands joined with `bitwise_or`, then intersect it with a workspace mask using `bitwise_and`.

hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((120, 160, 3), (30, 30, 200), dtype=np.uint8)
workspace = np.zeros((120, 160), np.uint8)
workspace[40:100, 20:140] = 255

hsv = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

low_band = cv2.inRange(hsv, np.array([0, 120, 70], np.uint8), np.array([10, 255, 255], np.uint8))
high_band = cv2.inRange(hsv, np.array([170, 120, 70], np.uint8), np.array([179, 255, 255], np.uint8))

red = cv2.bitwise_or(low_band, high_band)
red = cv2.bitwise_and(red, workspace)

print(int(cv2.countNonZero(red)))
lessons.hint: The OR joins the two hue bands, and the AND with the workspace mask throws away everything outside the table.

lessons.title: Counting White
lessons.goal: Turn a mask into a scalar sensor reading with countNonZero and a coverage ratio.
lessons.theory:
A mask is an image, and a robot's control loop wants a number. `cv2.countNonZero(mask)` gives you how many pixels passed the gate, and dividing by `mask.size` gives coverage as a fraction between 0 and 1.

That single number is a surprisingly good sensor. A coverage above 0.02 in the bottom strip means the line is still under the rover. A coverage above 0.4 across the whole frame means an object is right in front of the lens, close enough to stop. A coverage of exactly 0 for ten consecutive frames means the target is lost and the search behaviour should take over.

Always threshold coverage, never raw pixel counts. A count of 900 means something entirely different at 640x480 and at 1920x1080, and someone will change the resolution eventually. Ratios survive that change, magic counts do not.
lessons.task: Write `coverage(mask)` returning the fraction of non zero pixels, then use it on the bottom third of the mask and print whether the line is present with a threshold of 0.02.
lessons.starter:

import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((300, 400), np.uint8)
mask[250:290, 180:220] = 255

def coverage(mask):
    # TODO: fraction of white pixels
    return 0.0

print(round(coverage(mask), 4))
lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((300, 400), np.uint8)
mask[250:290, 180:220] = 255

def coverage(mask):
    if mask.size == 0:
        return 0.0
    return cv2.countNonZero(mask) / float(mask.size)

height = mask.shape[0]
strip = mask[(height * 2) // 3:, :]
line_present = coverage(strip) > 0.02

print(round(coverage(strip), 4), line_present)
lessons.hint: `mask.size` is the total pixel count, so the ratio is the count of white divided by it.

lessons.title: The Biggest Blob
lessons.goal: Label connected regions with connectedComponentsWithStats and keep the largest one.
lessons.theory:
A color gate rarely returns one clean region. It returns the cone you want plus a reflection on the floor plus three pixels of noise. `cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask)` separates them: it returns the number of labels, a label image, a stats array and a centroids array.

The stats array has one row per label with `[x, y, width, height, area]`, and the constants `cv2.CC_STAT_AREA` and friends index the columns readably. **Label 0 is always the background**, so any loop over components starts at 1. Forgetting that is the classic bug: the background is the largest region in almost every frame, so the detector reports the whole image as the target.

Centroids come out for free in the same call, as floats, which is more accurate than the integer center of a bounding box. That is your first real object position, and the next lesson turns it into a steering command.
lessons.task: Find the largest non background component in the mask, and print its area and its centroid.

import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
mask[20:40, 20:40] = 255
mask[100:160, 80:170] = 255

# TODO: label the components and pick the biggest one that is not background
best_area = 0

print(best_area)

import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
mask[20:40, 20:40] = 255
mask[100:160, 80:170] = 255

count, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask, connectivity=8)

best_area = 0
best_centroid = None
for i in range(1, count):
    area = int(stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA])
    if area > best_area:
        best_area = area
        best_centroid = centroids[i]

print(best_area, None if best_centroid is None else [round(float(c), 1) for c in best_centroid])

lessons.title: The Steering Number
lessons.goal: Convert a blob centroid into a normalized lateral error the control loop can use.
lessons.theory:
Vision ends where control begins, and the handover is a single normalized number. Take the centroid x, subtract the image center x, divide by half the width. You get an **error** between -1 and 1: negative means the target is to the left, zero means dead ahead, one means at the right edge. The centroid and the size of each blob come out of `cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats`, which hands you a stats table you read by column: `cv2.CC_STAT_AREA` is the pixel count of a label, the value the `min_area` filter compares against.

Normalizing is what makes the number portable. A PID gain tuned on a 640 pixel wide frame keeps working when you switch to a 1280 pixel camera, because the error no longer carries units of pixels. This is the same reason the previous lesson used coverage instead of counts.

The missing case matters as much as the present one. When no blob passes the area filter, do not return 0, because 0 means perfectly centered and the robot will drive straight into whatever it cannot see. Return `None` and let the behaviour layer decide between coasting, stopping or searching.

A guard that never fires is a guard you have not tested. Run the function on the case it is written to reject as well as on the case it answers, in the same output, and the reader can see the branch taken rather than take your word for it.

Three frames are enough here: a blob of 3600 pixels that clears the filter, a speck of 100 pixels that does not, and an empty frame. The last two have to come back `None` for different reasons, one rejected by area and one with nothing to reject, and a version that returns 0 for either looks identical to a version that works until the rover hits something.

import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)
mask[120:180, 200:260] = 255

speck = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)
speck[120:130, 200:210] = 255

empty = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)

def steering_error(mask, min_area=200):
    count, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask, connectivity=8)
    best_area = 0
    best_x = None
    for i in range(1, count):
        area = int(stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA])
        if area >= min_area and area > best_area:
            best_area = area
            best_x = float(centroids[i][0])
    if best_x is None:
        return None
    half_width = mask.shape[1] / 2.0
    return (best_x - half_width) / half_width

for name, frame in (("blob", mask), ("speck", speck), ("empty", empty)):
    result = steering_error(frame)
    print(name, "error", None if result is None else round(result, 3))
lessons.hint: Keep half the frame width in `half_width`, since it is both the center and the divisor, and the empty case has to return `None`, not zero. If the speck comes back with a number instead of `None` the area comparison is running the wrong way round.

lessons.title: Salt on the Mask
lessons.goal: Recognise the three failure shapes of a raw binary mask before trying to fix them.
lessons.theory:
A mask straight out of `inRange` has three defects and each one has its own cure. **Salt** is isolated white pixels in the background, from sensor noise and JPEG artifacts. **Holes** are black pixels inside the object, from a specular highlight that blew past the value ceiling. **Bridges** are thin white threads joining two objects that should be separate, from a shadow that happens to match the hue.

Naming the defect before reaching for a function is the whole discipline of morphology. Erosion kills salt and bridges but shrinks the object. Dilation fills holes and joins bridges. Opening and closing combine them so the object keeps its size. Applying the wrong one makes the mask worse in a way that is hard to see until the centroid jumps.

Measure, do not squint. The count of connected components tells you about salt and bridges, and comparing the filled contour area against the raw pixel count tells you about holes. That raw count is `cv2.countNonZero(mask)`, a one argument call that returns how many pixels are not zero, which on a binary mask is exactly the white area in pixels. This lesson builds that measurement so the rest of the chapter has a scoreboard.

mask[40:80, 40:80] = 255
mask[10, 10] = 255
mask[55:60, 55:60] = 0

def mask_report(mask):

import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((120, 120), np.uint8)
mask[40:80, 40:80] = 255
mask[10, 10] = 255
mask[55:60, 55:60] = 0

def mask_report(mask):
    count, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask, connectivity=8)
    areas = [int(stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]) for i in range(1, count)]
    real = [a for a in areas if a > 5]
    return {
        "components": len(real),
        "white": int(cv2.countNonZero(mask)),
        "largest": max(areas) if areas else 0,

lessons.title: Eating the Edges
lessons.goal: Erode a mask to remove isolated noise, and measure how much the object shrank.
lessons.theory:
**Erosion** slides a kernel over the mask and keeps a pixel white only if every pixel under the kernel is white. A 3x3 kernel therefore strips one pixel from every boundary, and anything thinner than the kernel disappears entirely. That is exactly what kills salt and cuts one pixel bridges.

The cost is real: a circular blob 40 pixels wide comes out 38 pixels wide after one iteration with a 3x3 kernel, and its area drops by about 10 percent. If a later stage measures the part to decide whether it is the 20 millimetre bolt or the 25 millimetre one, erosion alone will lie to it.

`cv2.erode(mask, kernel, iterations=n)` with n iterations of a 3x3 kernel is roughly one pass of a (2n+1)x(2n+1) kernel and is usually faster. Prefer more iterations of a small kernel over one pass of a large one.

lessons.title: Growing Back
lessons.goal: Dilate a mask to fill small holes and reconnect a broken object.
lessons.theory:
**Dilation** is the mirror of erosion: a pixel becomes white if any pixel under the kernel is white. Boundaries grow by one pixel per iteration, small holes close, and two nearby fragments merge into one component.

On a robot, dilation rescues masks broken by specular highlights. A glossy black conveyor belt reflects the ceiling lights and the belt mask comes out with white gaps. Two iterations of dilation close the gaps so the contour finder returns one belt instead of eleven fragments.

Dilation also merges things you wanted separate. Two bolts lying 4 pixels apart become one blob after 2 iterations, and the centroid lands in the empty space between them. When separation matters, dilate as little as possible and lean on closing instead, which is the next pair of lessons.

lessons.title: Open for Noise
lessons.goal: Remove speckle without shrinking the object using morphological opening.
lessons.theory:
**Opening** is erosion followed by dilation with the same kernel, and OpenCV gives it to you as `cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)`. The kernel is not a number, it is a small binary image you build with `cv2.getStructuringElement(shape, ksize)`, passing a shape flag such as `cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE` or `cv2.MORPH_RECT` and a size tuple. The erosion deletes anything thinner than the kernel, and the dilation grows back what survived. Speckle is gone and the object is roughly its original size.

Roughly, not exactly. Sharp corners come back rounded, because the dilation cannot recreate detail the erosion destroyed. That is acceptable for a centroid and unacceptable if you are about to measure a corner angle. Order your pipeline so the measurement that needs sharp geometry runs before the cleanup that rounds it.

Opening is the default first move on any `inRange` mask. A 5x5 elliptical kernel and one iteration removes the vast majority of color noise on a typical webcam frame and costs under a millisecond at 640x480.

lessons.title: Close for Holes
lessons.goal: Fill holes and gaps inside an object with morphological closing.
lessons.theory:
**Closing** is dilation followed by erosion, and you ask for it through the same entry point as opening with the operation flag swapped: `cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)`. The dilation swallows holes and gaps smaller than the kernel, the erosion returns the outer boundary to where it was. The object keeps its outline and loses its interior defects.

This is the fix for the specular highlight problem. A red plastic part under an LED ring has a white spot in the middle that fails the hue test, so the mask has a hole and `contourArea` reports the object as a ring. Closing with a kernel larger than the highlight repairs it, and the area measurement becomes trustworthy again.

The kernel size is set by the largest defect you must close, not by taste. Measure the widest hole in pixels and round up to the next odd number strictly above it: a 10 pixel hole needs 11, and 9 is not enough. Watch out for the half fix, because it is the one that fools people. An undersized kernel still raises the white count, since it nibbles the rim of the hole, so the print looks like progress while the hole is still sitting there. Only the count reaching the full area of the solid shape proves the hole is gone. A kernel much larger than needed will also swallow the real gap between two parts touching at a corner.

lessons.title: The Shape of the Kernel
lessons.goal: Choose between rectangular, elliptical and cross kernels based on the object geometry.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.getStructuringElement(shape, size)` builds the kernel, and the shape argument changes the result more than beginners expect. `MORPH_RECT` is a full block, it is the most aggressive and turns round objects square. `MORPH_ELLIPSE` is a disc, it preserves curvature and is the right default for parts, balls and cones. `MORPH_CROSS` only touches the four axis neighbours, so it is the gentlest and the cheapest.

Anisotropic kernels are a real tool, not a curiosity. A 1x15 rectangular kernel used with closing joins the dashes of a dashed floor line into one continuous line without merging it with the line in the next lane. A 15x1 kernel does the same vertically for a rack upright.

Building the kernel once outside the loop matters. `getStructuringElement` allocates, and calling it per frame at 30 Hz for three different stages is pure waste on an embedded board.

lessons.title: The Outline Operator
lessons.goal: Extract a one pixel outline from a mask with the morphological gradient.
lessons.theory:
The **morphological gradient** is the dilation minus the erosion, `cv2.MORPH_GRADIENT`. What survives is exactly the boundary, a band whose thickness equals the kernel size minus one. It is an edge detector that only works on binary or very flat images, but on those it is faster and more predictable than Canny.

It earns its place in two situations. Drawing a debug overlay where you want the object outlined without hiding the pixels underneath, and feeding a Hough transform that expects thin edges when your input is already a clean binary mask, for instance a floor line you segmented by color.

The gradient of a noisy mask is a disaster, because every speckle contributes its own tiny ring. Clean it with an opening first, which is the same `morphologyEx` call with `cv2.MORPH_OPEN` in place of `cv2.MORPH_GRADIENT`. The order cleanup then gradient is not optional, it is the difference between 4 contours and 400.

lessons.title: Top Hat Under Uneven Light
lessons.goal: Separate bright and dark details from an uneven background with the top hat and black hat transforms.
lessons.theory:
**Top hat** is the image minus its opening, `cv2.MORPH_TOPHAT`. The opening with a large kernel is an estimate of the slow varying background, so subtracting it leaves only bright details smaller than the kernel. **Black hat**, `cv2.MORPH_BLACKHAT`, is the closing minus the image and does the same for dark details.

This is how you read a laser engraved serial number off a curved metal part under a lamp that lights one side. Global thresholding fails because the bright side of the part is brighter than the dark side's marks. Black hat with a 25x25 kernel removes the illumination gradient completely and leaves the marks, and then even a fixed threshold works.

Unlike adaptive thresholding, top hat leaves you a grayscale image, so you can still threshold it however you like afterwards, or feed it to Otsu, which now sees a genuinely bimodal histogram. Otsu is a flag rather than a function: pass `cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU` to `cv2.threshold` and the threshold value you hand it is ignored, because `cv2.THRESH_OTSU` reads the split point off the histogram itself.

The pair is only convincing side by side, because each hat has to find its own mark and ignore the other one. The frame below carries a dark mark on its bright half and a bright mark on its dark half, both of them invisible to any single global cut: the bright mark is darker than the far side of the illumination ramp, and the dark mark is brighter than the near side. Run both hats and a plain global Otsu on the same frame and the third one lights up tens of thousands of pixels of gradient while missing the mark that matters.

import cv2
import numpy as np

gray = np.tile(np.linspace(60, 240, 300).astype(np.uint8), (200, 1))
gray[90:110, 100:140] = 30
gray[130:150, 40:80] = 170

bright_box = (slice(125, 155), slice(35, 85))
dark_box = (slice(85, 115), slice(95, 145))

kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_RECT, (25, 25))

_, bright_marks = cv2.threshold(cv2.morphologyEx(gray, cv2.MORPH_TOPHAT, kernel), 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

lessons.title: The Clean Mask Pipeline
lessons.goal: Assemble color gate, opening, closing and area filtering into one reusable function.
lessons.theory:
Every detector in the rest of this course starts from the same five steps: blur, convert to HSV, gate the color, open to remove speckle, close to fill holes. Writing that once as `clean_mask(frame, lower, upper)` is not tidiness, it is the difference between tuning one function and hunting five copies of the same numbers.

Order is fixed and each step earns its place. Blur before the gate, so noise does not flicker across the hue boundary. Open before close, because closing speckle first turns it into bigger speckle. Area filtering last, since only after cleaning are the areas meaningful. In code that is `cv2.morphologyEx` twice, `cv2.MORPH_OPEN` with the small ellipse and then `cv2.MORPH_CLOSE` with the bigger one.

Give the function an escape hatch: return the intermediate masks when a `debug` flag is set. On a robot you will need to see which stage destroyed the object, and rebuilding the pipeline by hand at 2 am on the workshop floor is how people ship the wrong fix.

import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.full((160, 160, 3), (30, 160, 240), dtype=np.uint8)
lower = np.array([10, 120, 70], np.uint8)
upper = np.array([30, 255, 255], np.uint8)

OPEN_KERNEL = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (5, 5))
CLOSE_KERNEL = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (7, 7))

def clean_mask(frame, lower, upper, min_area=150):
    blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(frame, (5, 5), 0)
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(blurred, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
    mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower, upper)
    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, OPEN_KERNEL)
    mask = cv2.morphologyEx(mask, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, CLOSE_KERNEL)

    count, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(mask, connectivity=8)
    for i in range(1, count):
        if stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA] < min_area:
            mask[labels == i] = 0
    return mask

print(cv2.countNonZero(clean_mask(frame, lower, upper)))
lessons.hint: `mask[labels == i] = 0` erases one labelled component in a single NumPy assignment.

lessons.title: Tracing the Border
lessons.goal: Extract object outlines from a binary mask with findContours and draw them.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.findContours(mask, mode, method)` walks the boundary of every white region and returns a list of point arrays, each of shape `(n, 1, 2)`. That odd middle axis is a legacy of the C++ API and you will index past it constantly with `contour[:, 0, :]`.

The mode decides what you get. `cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL` returns only outermost contours, which is what a part detector wants. `cv2.RETR_TREE` returns everything including holes, plus a hierarchy array describing who contains whom. The method decides how points are stored: `cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE` collapses straight runs into their endpoints and typically stores a rectangle in 4 points instead of 400.

Contours are the bridge from pixels to geometry. Everything in this chapter, area, orientation, corner count, centroid, is a function computed on these point arrays, and they are cheap because a contour is a few hundred numbers instead of a few hundred thousand pixels.

lessons.title: Size Is the First Filter
lessons.goal: Reject noise contours by area with contourArea and a physically justified threshold.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.contourArea(contour)` returns the enclosed area in pixels. Sorting contours by it and keeping the ones above a floor removes almost all false detections in one line, and it is the first filter every practical detector applies.

Derive the floor from physics, not from trial and error. If the smallest part you must see is 15 millimetres across, the camera sees 0.4 millimetres per pixel at the working distance, then the part is about 37 pixels wide and its area is over 1000 pixels. Anything under 300 is not a part. Written that way, the constant survives a lens change because you recompute it instead of guessing again.

An upper bound is just as useful. A contour covering 60 percent of the frame is not a bolt, it is the shadow of the robot arm or a lighting failure that made the whole gate saturate. Detectors that only have a lower bound behave catastrophically when the light goes wrong.

lessons.title: The Bounding Box
lessons.goal: Compute an axis aligned bounding box from a contour and use it to crop the object.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.boundingRect(contour)` returns `(x, y, w, h)`, the smallest axis aligned rectangle containing the contour. It is the cheapest description of where an object is, and it is the format every tracker, every neural detector and every ROI crop in OpenCV expects.

Axis aligned is both its strength and its limit. For a box on a conveyor moving straight it is exact. For the same box rotated 45 degrees the rectangle is nearly twice the object's area and its center is still correct, but its width no longer means the object's width. Do not measure parts with it.

The aspect ratio `w / h` is a free classifier. A standing bottle and a lying bottle produce very different ratios, and on a picking cell that single number is often enough to decide whether the gripper approaches from the top or the side.

import cv2
import numpy as np

frame = np.zeros((200, 300, 3), np.uint8)
mask = np.zeros((200, 300), np.uint8)
mask[60:140, 80:200] = 255

contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
biggest = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(biggest)
aspect = w / float(h)

pad = 5
height, width = frame.shape[:2]
x0 = max(0, x - pad)
y0 = max(0, y - pad)
x1 = min(width, x + w + pad)
y1 = min(height, y + h + pad)
crop = frame[y0:y1, x0:x1]

print(round(aspect, 2), crop.shape)

lessons.title: The Tilted Box
lessons.goal: Get the object true width, height and orientation with minAreaRect.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.minAreaRect(contour)` returns `((cx, cy), (w, h), angle)`, the smallest rectangle of any orientation that contains the contour. Unlike the axis aligned box, its width and height are the object's real dimensions and its angle is the object's orientation.

That angle is what a gripper needs. To pick a rectangular part you rotate the wrist to align the fingers with the short side, and the short side direction comes straight out of this call. `cv2.boxPoints(rect)` converts the result to four corner points for drawing or for further geometry.

The angle convention bites everyone. In OpenCV 4.5 and later the angle is in the range 0 to 90 and which side is called width depends on the contour, so a part slowly rotating past a boundary makes the reported angle jump by 90 degrees. Normalise it yourself: define the angle by the longer side and wrap it into a fixed range before it reaches the control loop.

lessons.goal: Simplify a contour with approxPolyDP and classify a shape by its vertex count.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.approxPolyDP(contour, epsilon, closed)` runs the Ramer Douglas Peucker algorithm: it throws away points that lie within `epsilon` of the line joining their neighbours. A noisy 400 point outline of a triangle collapses to 3 points.

A fixed 5 pixels would over simplify a small part and under simplify a large one, and the vertex count would depend on how far the camera was.

The vertex count is then a shape label: 3 is a triangle, 4 a quadrilateral, and anything above 8 with a high circularity is a circle. On a sorting cell this replaces a classifier network entirely, runs in microseconds, and never hallucinates a class it was not shown.

import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
cv2.fillPoly(mask, [np.array([[50, 30], [160, 60], [120, 160], [40, 130]])], 255)
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)

def classify(contour):
    perimeter = cv2.arcLength(contour, True)
    if perimeter <= 0:
        return "unknown"
    approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(contour, 0.02 * perimeter, True)
    vertices = len(approx)
    if vertices == 3:
        return "triangle"
    if vertices == 4:
        return "quad"
    if vertices == 5:
        return "pentagon"
    if vertices >= 8:
        return "round"
    return "unknown"

print(classify(contours[0]), len(cv2.approxPolyDP(contours[0], 0.02 * cv2.arcLength(contours[0], True), True)))
lessons.hint: `cv2.arcLength(contour, True)` gives the closed perimeter, and two percent of it is the usual epsilon.

lessons.title: The Rubber Band
lessons.goal: Compute the convex hull and use solidity to detect concave or damaged parts.
lessons.theory:
The **convex hull** is the shape a rubber band takes around the contour: `cv2.convexHull(contour)`. Every dent is bridged over. Comparing the contour to its hull is how you measure how dented it is.

**Solidity** is the ratio `contourArea(contour) / contourArea(hull)`. A solid rectangle scores near 1.0. A gear, a bracket with a cutout or a part with a broken corner scores clearly below. On an inspection cell a solidity threshold at 0.92 separates good parts from chipped ones without knowing anything about the part's design.

`cv2.convexityDefects` goes further and returns each dent with its start point, end point, deepest point and depth. It needs the hull computed with `returnPoints=False` so the result is indices, which is the single most common mistake with this function. Counting deep defects is the classic way to count fingers on a hand or teeth on a gear.

import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
cv2.fillPoly(mask, [np.array([[40, 40], [160, 40], [160, 160], [100, 100], [40, 160]])], 255)
contour = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)[0][0]

lessons.title: The Center of Mass
lessons.goal: Compute a subpixel centroid from image moments and guard the zero area case.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.moments(contour)` returns the raw moments of the shape. The centroid is `cx = m10 / m00` and `cy = m01 / m00`, where `m00` is the area. Unlike a bounding box center, this is the true center of mass and it is **subpixel accurate**, which matters when the vision output feeds a servo loop.

`m00` can be zero. A degenerate contour, a line one pixel wide, an empty mask, all produce a division by zero that crashes the node mid mission. Every production implementation of this checks `m00` before dividing, and there is no excuse for the version that does not.

Moments also work directly on a binary mask, not only on a contour, which is faster when you already have a clean single object mask and do not need the outline at all. Higher order moments give orientation, and Hu moments give the seven values used for rotation invariant shape matching in the next lesson.

A guard that never fires is a guard you have not tested. Run the function on the case it is written to reject as well as on the case it answers, in the same output, and the reader can see the branch taken rather than take your word for it.

The degenerate contour is easy to build: three collinear points enclose no area, so `m00` comes back as exactly 0.0 and the guarded version returns `None` where the unguarded one raises. Print `m00` next to each answer and the reason for the branch is on screen with it.

import cv2
import numpy as np

mask = np.zeros((200, 200), np.uint8)
cv2.circle(mask, (120, 80), 40, 255, -1)
disc = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)[0][0]
flat = np.array([[[10, 10]], [[60, 10]], [[110, 10]]], np.int32)

def centroid(contour):
    m = cv2.moments(contour)
    if m["m00"] == 0:
        return None
    return (m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"])

for name, contour in (("disc", disc), ("three collinear points", flat)):
    area = cv2.moments(contour)["m00"]
    result = centroid(contour)
    print(name, "m00", area, "->", None if result is None else (round(result[0], 2), round(result[1], 2)))

lessons.title: How Round Is Round
lessons.goal: Compute circularity from area and perimeter to separate round parts from angular ones.
lessons.theory:
**Circularity** is `4 * pi * area / perimeter ** 2`. A perfect circle gives 1.0, a square about 0.785, a long thin sliver approaches 0. It is a single scale invariant number that says how compact a shape is, and it costs two calls you already know: `cv2.contourArea(contour)` for the numerator and `cv2.arcLength(contour, True)` for the perimeter, where that second argument declares the curve closed so the segment from the last point back to the first is counted.

On a picking cell that separates washers from square nuts it does the job that people reach for a classifier network to do. It is also the sanity check that catches a merged blob: two touching washers have roughly double the area but far more than double the wiggle in the perimeter, so circularity collapses and you know the segmentation failed before you send a grasp command.

Pixellation biases it downward for small contours, because a staircase boundary has a longer perimeter than the true curve. Below about 20 pixels of diameter the number stops being reliable, which is another reason the area floor from earlier in this chapter exists.

lessons.title: Sorting the Bin
lessons.goal: Combine area, circularity, solidity and centroid into one detector that reports labelled parts.
lessons.theory:
This is the first complete detector of the course. Input is a frame, output is a list of dicts with a label, a centroid, an area and an orientation. The orientation is not the axis aligned bounding box, it comes from `cv2.minAreaRect(contour)`, which returns the smallest rotated rectangle that still contains the contour as `((cx, cy), (w, h), angle)`, so the angle belongs to the part and not to the image axes. Everything downstream, the gripper planner, the logger, the debug overlay, consumes that list and nothing else.

The design rule is that features are computed once and decisions are made from named variables, not from nested function calls inside an `if`. When the cell starts rejecting good parts at 3 am, you want to log `area=1240 circ=0.61 sol=0.88` and see immediately which threshold fired. A one line boolean expression tells you nothing.

Sort the output by area descending and cap the list length. A vision node that returns 400 detections after a lighting failure will stall whatever consumes it, and the top few are the only ones any real robot acts on.

lessons.solution:
import cv2
import numpy as np
import math

mask = np.zeros((240, 320), np.uint8)
cv2.circle(mask, (80, 120), 35, 255, -1)
mask[60:180, 180:280] = 255

def detect_parts(mask, min_area=300, max_results=10):
    contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
    parts = []
    for contour in contours:
        area = cv2.contourArea(contour)
        if area < min_area:
            continue
        perimeter = cv2.arcLength(contour, True)
        if perimeter <= 0:
            continue
        circ = 4.0 * math.pi * area / (perimeter * perimeter)
        hull_area = cv2.contourArea(cv2.convexHull(contour))
        solidity = area / hull_area if hull_area > 0 else 0.0
        m = cv2.moments(contour)
        if m["m00"] == 0:
            continue
        center = (m["m10"] / m["m00"], m["m01"] / m["m00"])
        (_, _), (w, h), raw_angle = cv2.minAreaRect(contour)
        angle = (raw_angle if w >= h else raw_angle + 90.0) % 180.0

        if circ > 0.85:
            label = "washer"
        elif solidity < 0.9:
            label = "bracket"
        else:
            label = "block"

        parts.append({
            "label": label,
            "center": (round(center[0], 1), round(center[1], 1)),
            "area": int(area),
            "angle": round(angle, 1),
        })

    parts.sort(key=lambda p: p["area"], reverse=True)
    return parts[:max_results]

for part in detect_parts(mask):
    print(part)
lessons.hint: Compute every feature into its own variable first, then write the label decision as a plain if chain over those variables.

lessons.title: Blur Before You Look
lessons.goal: Suppress sensor noise with Gaussian, median and bilateral filters and know which one to use.
lessons.theory:
Every edge detector is a derivative, and derivatives amplify noise. A single hot pixel with a value 30 above its neighbours produces a gradient bigger than the real edge of a dark part on a gray table. Blurring first is not optional, it is part of the operator.

Three filters cover the cases. `cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)` is the default, cheap and smooth, and a sigma of 0 makes OpenCV derive sigma from the kernel size. `cv2.medianBlur` is the one that removes salt and pepper noise from a bad USB cable, because a median ignores outliers instead of averaging them in. `cv2.bilateralFilter` smooths flat regions while keeping edges sharp, at ten times the cost, which is worth it before a measurement and never inside a 30 Hz loop.

Bigger kernels destroy the features you are looking for. A 15x15 Gaussian erases a 10 pixel wide floor line completely, and then Canny finds nothing and you blame Canny. Match the kernel to the smallest feature you need to keep.

lessons.title: The Slope of Brightness
lessons.goal: Compute horizontal and vertical derivatives with the Sobel operator.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0, ksize=3)` computes the derivative along x: how fast brightness changes as you move right. The 3x3 kernel combines a derivative in one direction with a small smoothing in the other, which is why Sobel is more robust than a raw difference of neighbours.

The output depth argument is where people go wrong. A derivative is **signed**: a dark to light edge is positive, light to dark is negative. The strip below is a bright band on a dark field, so it carries one edge of each kind and the printed extremes are -600.0 and 600.0. Ask for `cv2.CV_8U` instead and every negative value is clipped to zero, which does not dim the falling edge, it deletes it: of the 800 edge pixels the band produces, the 400 on its trailing side stop existing. Compute in `CV_64F` or `CV_32F`, then take the absolute value and convert with `cv2.convertScaleAbs` only for display.

On a robot the x derivative alone is often the whole answer. A vertical rack upright, a door frame, a wall corner, all produce strong `dx` and nearly zero `dy`, which is why the band below leaves `dy` flat at 0.0, so summing `abs(dx)` per column gives you a one dimensional signal whose peaks are the uprights, at a fraction of the cost of a full edge detector.

lessons.title: Magnitude and Direction
lessons.goal: Turn the two Sobel derivatives into gradient magnitude and angle with cartToPolar.
lessons.theory:
The two derivatives form a vector per pixel. Its length is the **edge strength**, its angle is the **edge direction** rotated by 90 degrees. `cv2.cartToPolar(dx, dy, angleInDegrees=True)` computes both in one pass, faster and more accurate than doing it with NumPy square roots.

Direction is the part people leave on the table. Knowing that an edge runs at 3 degrees off horizontal lets you keep only the edges that could belong to the floor line and discard the rack legs before any Hough transform runs. Histogramming the angles over the whole frame gives you the dominant orientation of the scene, which is how a rover detects that it is not aligned with the corridor.

Angles are circular, so 179 and 1 degree are two degrees apart, not 178. Any averaging or clustering of edge directions must be done on the unit vectors or with a modulo aware distance, and forgetting that produces a heading estimate that swings wildly whenever the true angle sits near the wrap point.

A direction filter can only be judged on a frame that contains edges it should throw away. Test it on a scene with a horizontal bar and an upright post in it and print both counts, the strong gradient pixels and the ones the angle test kept. If the two numbers are equal your filter is decoration: every strong pixel in the frame already pointed the way you asked for, and the same code would pass with the angle test deleted.

lessons.title: The Second Derivative
lessons.goal: Use the Laplacian for zero crossing edges and as a focus measure.
lessons.theory:
The **Laplacian** sums the second derivatives in x and y. Where Sobel peaks at an edge, the Laplacian crosses zero, which in principle gives sharper localisation. In practice it is twice as sensitive to noise as the first derivative, which is why Canny uses gradients and not this.

Its real job on a robot is measuring focus. The variance of the Laplacian over a frame is high when the image is sharp and collapses when it is blurred, because blur destroys high frequencies. A gripper camera on a focus motor sweeps focus and keeps the position that maximises `cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F).var()`.

That same number is a health check worth logging every frame. A sudden drop means the lens fogged, a drop of water landed on the housing, or the camera is vibrating past its exposure time. Detecting that in the vision node is far better than shipping garbage detections downstream and wondering why the arm missed.

lessons.title: Canny and the Two Thresholds
lessons.goal: Detect thin connected edges with Canny and understand hysteresis thresholding.
lessons.theory:
`cv2.Canny(gray, low, high)` does four things: it smooths, computes gradients, thins every ridge to one pixel through non maximum suppression, and then applies **hysteresis**. Any pixel above `high` is an edge. Any pixel between `low` and `high` is an edge only if it connects to one that is above `high`.

That second rule is the whole point. A single threshold either breaks long edges into dashes or floods the frame with noise. Hysteresis keeps faint continuations of strong edges while rejecting isolated faint pixels, which is why Canny output is usable by Hough and raw gradient magnitude is not.

The usual starting ratio is `high = 3 * low`, applied to an already blurred grayscale image. Feed Canny a color frame and it runs on each channel and merges, which is slower and noisier. Feed it a binary mask and it just outlines the mask, which you already know how to do more cheaply with the morphological gradient.

A frame made of one clean high contrast shape cannot show you any of this. Every pixel on it clears `high`, so the count comes out the same whatever you pass as `low`, and the lower threshold might as well not be an argument. What proves hysteresis is a bar that fades along its length, bright enough to seed at one end and only faint at the other, next to an isolated bar of that same faint contrast. The faded end survives because it is connected. The lonely bar, identical in contrast, does not.

lessons.title: Thresholds Without Guessing
lessons.goal: Derive Canny thresholds from the image median so they survive a lighting change.
lessons.theory:
Hardcoded Canny thresholds are tuned for one exposure. Drive the robot from a lit aisle into a shadowed one and the same 50 and 150 return an empty edge map. The standard fix, published by Adrian Rosebrock and used everywhere since, derives them from the median: `low = max(0, 0.66 * median)` and `high = min(255, 1.33 * median)`.

The median is the right statistic because it ignores the bright specular outliers that would drag a mean upward. One `np.median` call per frame costs almost nothing next to the Canny itself.

Auto thresholds are not magic, they are one less thing to retune. Log the chosen pair every few seconds. When the edge count goes to zero and the log shows a median of 8, you know the exposure collapsed, not that the algorithm broke, and the fix is on the camera side.
